Spread Betting vs. CFDs: What’s The Difference?
Vantage Editorial Team >
11 August 2026
|
Academy
|
12 min read
Vantage Editorial Team >
View Profile
Vantage is a global, multi-asset broker with a team of in-house writers and market analysts who produce educational and insightful trading content for traders of all levels.
CFD trading and spread betting are similar. Both let you trade on price movements without owning the underlying asset, giving you access to markets like forex, commodities, indices, and shares.
But what’s the difference between CFD trading and spread betting?
While the trading experience appears similar, there are differences in some areas including taxation, trading cost, position sizing, and availability. These may affect how you trade and how you decide which product suits your goals better.
This article seeks to explain the key differences between
CFDs
and
spread betting
in simple terms, including how each product works, what’s different between the two, and what to consider before deciding which one is right for you.
Key Takeaways
CFDs and spread betting both let you trade on price movements without owning the underlying asset.
The main differences are tax treatment, trading costs, position sizing, and country availability.
The trading experience is very similar, but the way trades are structured and priced is different.
Neither product is better for everyone. The right choice depends on each individual trading goal, preferred trading style, and the features offered by different brokers.
Why Do CFD Trading and Spread Betting Seem So Similar?
In practice, CFD trading and spread betting share the same features, which is why on some trading platforms, the overall trading experience feels remarkably similar.
Both products are leveraged derivatives, meaning you speculate on whether the price of an asset will rise or fall without taking ownership of the underlying asset. Instead of buying shares outright or exchanging physical commodities, you’re trading based on price movements in the market.
With CFDs and spread betting, you can typically:
Trade rising and falling markets by taking long or short positions.
Access a wide range of markets, including
forex
, commodities,
indices
, and shares.
Use leverage to gain greater market exposure with a smaller initial deposit (known as margin).
Pay overnight financing charges when holding leveraged positions beyond the trading.
From a day-to-day trading perspective, the differences may not be immediately obvious. You may use the same charts, place similar orders, and analyse the market in exactly the same way, regardless of which product you choose.
The key differences lie behind the scenes. CFDs and spread betting are structured differently, which affects how trades are priced, how positions are sized, where each product is available, and how profits may be treated for tax purposes. Understanding these distinctions can help you choose the product that best fits your trading objectives.
What Are The Biggest Differences Between CFDs And Spread Betting?
CFDs and spread betting may look similar, but there are a few key differences that can affect which product is right for your trading goals. The main ones are tax treatment, trading costs, position sizing, and availability.
1.
Tax Treatment
One of the biggest differences between CFDs and spread betting is how profits are taxed.
Spread betting profits are generally exempt from Capital Gain Tax and Stamp Duty, making it a popular choice for many traders. CFDs are also exempt from Stamp Duty because you don’t own the underlying asset, but do note that profits may be subject to Capital Gain Tax.
Tax treatment depends on your personal circumstances and can change over time. If you’re unsure how it applies to you, consider seeking independent tax advice from a licensed professional.
2.
Trading Costs
Both CFDs and spread betting involve trading costs, but they’re charged differently.
With CFDs, you’ll usually pay the spread. Depending on the market, such as
share CFDs
, you may also pay a commission. Overnight financing charges can also apply if you keep a leveraged position open beyond the trading day.
With spread betting, costs are usually built into the spread, so there’s often no separate commission. However, overnight financing charges may still apply to positions held overnight.
When comparing products, look at the overall cost of trading rather than focusing on a single fee.
3.
Position Sizing
The way you size a trade also differs. With CFDs, positions are usually measured in contracts, units, or lots. For example, you might buy 100 share CFDs or trade one forex lot.
With spread betting, you choose how much you want to stake for every basis point the market moves. If your stake is £5 per point, you’ll make or lose £5 for each point the market rises or falls.
Both approaches provide similar market exposure. The difference is simply how your position is measured.
4.
Product Availability
CFDs are widely available in many countries, subject to local regulations.
Spread betting is mainly available in the UK and Ireland because of its legal and tax treatment. As a result, not every broker offers both products.
If you have access to both, your decision will often come down to your trading goals, preferred pricing structure, and tax considerations rather than the markets you want to trade.
What Does the Same Trade Look Like as a CFD vs. as a Spread Bet?
A side-by-side example makes the differences easier to understand. Imagine you expect the
FTSE 100
to rise.
CFD Example
You open a CFD position worth
£2,000
. If the FTSE 100 increases by
2%
, your position gains around
2%
in value. Ignoring spreads, commissions, and overnight financing, your gains would be about
£40
.
Spread Betting Example
Instead, you place a spread bet at
£10 per point
. If the FTSE 100 moves
4 points
in your favour, you make
£40
. If it moves
4 points
against you, you lose
£40
.
In both examples, you’re trading the same market and aiming to profit from the same price movement. The main difference is how the trade is structured. CFDs use contracts or units, while spread betting is based on your chosen stake per basis point.
CFD Trading vs. Spread Betting: Pros and Cons
Both leveraged products offer access to the same financial markets, but each has its own advantages and drawbacks.
Table 1: Pros and Cons of CFD Trading
CFD Trading
Pros
Cons
Available in many countries where CFD trading is allowed.
Profits may be subject to Capital Gains Tax.
Widely offered across forex, indices, commodities, shares, and more.
Some markets may include commission charges, transaction fees, and other costs.
Familiar position sizing using contracts, units, or lots.
Overnight financing charges may apply.
May offer different tax treatment for trading gains and losses.
Leverage increases both potential gains and potential losses.
Table 1 breaks down the ins and outs of CFD trading, covering everything from its global reach to how positions are sized. To help you decide which approach aligns best with your goals, let’s look at the next table to compare how these factors differ when it comes to spread betting.
Table 2: Pros and Cons of Spread Betting
Spread Betting
Pros
Cons
Profits are generally exempt from Capital Gains Tax and Stamp Duty.
Only available in the UK and Ireland.
Costs are often included in the spread, with no separate commission on many markets.
Position sizing may feel unfamiliar if you’re used to trading shares or lots.
Simple stake-per-point sizing.
Overnight financing charges may apply.
Popular among traders looking for a straightforward way to speculate on price movements.
Leverage increases both potential gains and potential losses.
Spread Betting vs. CFDs: Which One Might Suit You?
Whether spread betting and/or CFDs are suitable for you would depend on what matters most to you.
Spread betting may be a good fit if you:
Value favourable tax treatment as part of your trading strategy.
Prefer sizing trades as a stake per basis point.
Want trading costs to be built into the spread rather than paying separate commissions on some markets.
CFD trading may be a good fit if you:
Prefer trading in contracts, units, or lots.
Want a product that’s widely available across international markets.
Already trade shares, forex, or other leveraged products using a more traditional trading structure.
Whichever you choose, compare the pricing, available markets, and trading tools offered by your broker before opening an account.
Frequently Asked Questions
What’s the main difference between CFDs and spread betting?
Both products let you speculate on price movements without owning the underlying asset. The biggest differences are tax treatment, trading costs, position sizing, and availability.
Is spread betting tax-free?
Spread betting profits are generally exempt from Capital Gains Tax and Stamp Duty. However, tax treatment depends on your personal circumstances and may change over time.
Which is cheaper: CFDs or spread betting?
Whether CFD trading or spread betting is cheaper would depend on the market and your broker’s pricing. CFDs may include commissions, while spread betting costs are usually built into the spread. Both may also charge overnight financing fees.
Can I trade the same markets with CFDs and spread betting?
In many cases, yes. Both products commonly offer access to forex, indices, commodities, and shares, although the exact range of markets varies by broker.
Do I own the underlying asset?
No. Both CFDs and spread betting are leveraged derivatives, so you’re trading on price movements rather than buying the underlying asset.
Can beginners trade CFDs or spread betting?
Yes, but both products use leverage, which increases both potential gains and losses. Before trading, make sure you understand the risks and use appropriate risk management tools.

Currency Pairs in Forex Explained: Major, Minor and Exotic Pairs (2027)
Vantage Editorial Team >
5 August 2026
|
Academy
|
45 min read
Vantage Editorial Team >
View Profile
Vantage is a global, multi-asset broker with a team of in-house writers and market analysts who produce educational and insightful trading content for traders of all levels.
Currency pairs are typically grouped into majors, minors or crosses, and exotics according to market convention, trading activity and liquidity. However, these labels are not universal. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) uses a separate regulatory classification consisting only of major and minor foreign-exchange pairs.
In the UK, retail traders commonly gain leveraged exposure to these exchange-rate movements through
contracts for difference
(CFDs), financial spread bets, and rolling spot forex products. These instruments allow traders to speculate on price movements without owning the underlying currencies. However, these are complex, high-risk products, and losses can occur rapidly because of leverage.
Forex trading remains popular in 2026, with OTC forex turnover reaching $9.6 trillion per day in April 2025 — up 28% from $7.5 trillion three years earlier, according to the Bank for International Settlements’ 2025 Triennial Survey.
1
This guide covers 16 widely followed currency pairs, organised using familiar market terminology: seven conventionally recognised US-dollar majors, five cross-currency (minor) pairs, and four emerging-market pairs commonly described as exotics. Each entry also identifies its FCA classification for UK retail-CFD purposes.
The following examples are for illustrative purposes only and do not represent actual trading recommendations.
Key Points
Learn how currency pairs are structured and how they function as the foundation of forex trading.
Explore 16 widely followed major, minor, and emerging-market forex pairs, including their market drivers and FCA classification in the UK.
Understand pip values, correlation between pairs, and how to match a pair to your trading style.
What Is a Currency Pair?
A currency pair shows the exchange rate between two currencies, made up of a
base currency
and a
quote currency
. The first currency listed is the base currency; the second is the quote currency, which shows how many units are needed to buy one unit of the base currency. For example, EUR/USD shows how many US dollars are needed to buy one euro.
There is no fixed number of currency pairs, since almost any two currencies can theoretically be paired. In practice, trading activity is concentrated in a smaller group. Market convention commonly discusses seven US-dollar majors, minor cross-currency pairs, and emerging-market or exotic pairs, while the FCA uses only major and minor classifications for UK retail-CFD rules.
Image 1: The Global Landscape of Forex Trading
How Forex Trading Works
Forex trading, or foreign exchange trading, involves buying one currency while selling another, or taking a position based on how one currency is expected to move relative to another. In the UK retail market, this exposure is commonly provided through
leveraged CFDs
, financial spread bets, or rolling spot forex products, meaning the trader may not own or take delivery of either currency.
The global foreign-exchange market operates predominantly over the counter rather than through one centralised exchange. In the UK, forex transactions are generally entered into with a broker or provider through an online platform, and the provider may act as the trader’s counterparty.
As the world’s largest financial market, forex trading is generally available from Sunday evening until Friday evening, although exact hours, pricing, and liquidity vary between providers, currencies, and public holidays.
Learn more in our detailed
forex CFD trading guide
.
How to Read Currency Pairs
Currencies covered by the International Organization for Standardisation (ISO) 4217 standard are assigned three-letter alphabetic codes, otherwise known as their currency codes. This normally consists of the first two letters corresponding to the relevant country code, while the third letter corresponds to the first letter of the currency’s name.
For instance, USD represents the US dollar and EUR represents the euro. However, note that this pattern does not apply uniformly to every currency.
Image 2: Base and quote currency example
Base Currency and Quote Currency
In any currency pair, the first currency listed is the base currency and the second is the quote currency. The exchange rate indicates how many units of the quote currency are needed to buy one unit of the base currency.
Using EUR/USD as an example:
EUR is the base currency.
USD is the quote currency.
If the quoted price reads $1.2042, this means that 1.2042 US dollars is needed to buy one euro. The actual price available to a trader may differ depending on whether they are buying or selling, because brokers normally display separate bid and ask prices.
Long and Short Positions
A position refers to a trader’s exposure to movements in a currency pair. An open position remains active until it is closed, expires, or is offset by another position. Its value may rise or fall as the exchange rate changes. In UK retail forex trading, exposure obtained through leveraged CFDs, financial spread bets, or rolling spot forex products generally doesn’t give the trader ownership of the underlying currencies.
Long Position
A trader takes a long position when they buy the base currency and sell the quote currency, expecting the base currency to appreciate in value against the quote currency.
Example: Going long on EUR/USD if the trader believes the euro will strengthen against the US dollar.
Short Position
A trader takes a short position when they sell the base currency and buy the quote currency, anticipating that the base currency will depreciate against the quote currency.
Example: Going short on GBP/USD if they expect sterling to fall in value against the US dollar.
If the market moves in the expected direction, the position may gain value. If it moves in the opposite direction, the trader may incur a loss. Leverage magnifies both outcomes.
Worked example:
Suppose you exchange €1,000 into US dollars for a holiday when the exchange rate is EUR/USD 1.10. Ignoring spreads and charges, you receive $1,100. If the exchange rate subsequently falls to EUR/USD 1.00, those $1,100 would convert back into €1,100 — a €100 gain before costs, because the US dollar strengthened against the euro while you held dollars. If the exchange rate had moved the other way, converting the dollars back could instead have produced a loss.
Actual consumer exchange rates also include spreads, fees or commissions, and may differ from wholesale market rates. The Bank of England confirms that market exchange rates form the basis of — but are not necessarily identical to — the rates consumers receive from banks and currency-exchange providers.
5
Bid Price, Ask Price and the Spread
A tradeable currency pair quotation normally displays two prices:
Bid Price:
The price at which the trader can sell the base currency — or open a short position with a broker.
Ask Price:
The price at which the trader can buy the base currency — or open a long position. In the UK, the ask price is also called the offer price.
Currency Pair
Bid Price
Ask Price
EUR/USD
1.4745
1.4746
In this illustrative example:
A trader looking to
go long
(buy EUR, sell USD) would do so at the ask price of 1.4746.
A trader looking to
go short
(sell EUR, buy USD) would do so at the bid price of 1.4745.
The difference between the bid and ask price is known as the spread. In this example, the spread is 1 pip (0.0001), which represents one component of the overall trading costs. Other potential costs include commission, overnight financing (aka swap fees), currency-conversion charges, and slippage.
Spread size generally varies by currency pair: highly traded, liquid majors such as EUR/USD typically carry some of the tightest bid-ask
spreads
, while less-liquid pairs — including exotic pairs with thinner trading volume — tend to carry wider spreads. Major news, public holidays, the daily market rollover and quieter trading periods can all affect spreads.
What Is a Pip?
A pip (“percentage in point”) is the standard unit used to measure a change in a currency pair’s exchange rate. For most pairs, one pip is a movement in the fourth decimal place (0.0001) — so if EUR/USD moves from 1.4745 to 1.4755, that’s a 10-pip move. Yen-based pairs are the main exception: because JPY is quoted to two decimal places rather than four, one pip on USD/JPY is a movement in the second decimal place (0.01).
Pip value — how much a one-pip move is worth in monetary terms — depends on the trade size (lot size), the currency pair, and the account’s base currency. Brokers typically display pip value alongside a trade ticket, and most trading platforms include a pip or margin calculator so traders don’t need to calculate it manually. Understanding pip value matters because it directly determines position size and potential profit or loss on a given move.
Major Currency Pairs
Currency Pair
Description
EUR/USD
Policy divergence (Fed vs ECB). Fell below parity in 2022 for the first time in 20 years. FCA classification: major.
GBP/USD
Sensitive to Bank of England and Federal Reserve policy expectations, UK and US economic data, and political or fiscal developments. FCA classification: major.
USD/JPY
Interest rate gap (Fed vs BoJ). Popular for carry trades when US-Japanese interest rate differentials widen. FCA classification: major.
USD/CHF
Swiss franc is widely regarded as a safe-haven currency. May strengthen during periods of heightened uncertainty, but this is not guaranteed. Also influenced by Federal Reserve, Swiss National Bank monetary policy, interest-rate expectations, and broader market conditions. FCA classification: major.
AUD/USD
Influenced by commodity prices, especially iron ore, Australia’s terms of trade, Chinese demand, and Reserve Bank of Australia policy. FCA classification: minor.
USD/CAD
Influenced by oil and other commodity prices, as well as Federal Reserve and Bank of Canada policy. Higher oil prices may support the CAD, but the relationship isn’t guaranteed. FCA classification: major.
NZD/USD
Influenced by New Zealand’s export outlook, including dairy prices, as well as Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) policy, overseas demand, and global risk sentiment. FCA classification: minor.
Under common market convention, the seven major currency pairs combine the US dollar with the euro, pound sterling, Japanese yen, Swiss franc, Australian dollar, Canadian dollar or New Zealand dollar. They are generally among the most actively traded forex pairs and often have relatively tight spreads, although actual spreads vary by provider and market conditions.
For UK retail-CFD rules, a major foreign-exchange pair is any pair formed from two currencies in the FCA’s six-currency list: USD, EUR, JPY, GBP, CAD and CHF. All other currency pairs are minor. Consequently, AUD/USD and NZD/USD are FCA minor pairs, even though market publications commonly include them among the seven majors. FCA rules require a minimum opening margin of 3.33% for major FX pairs and 5% for minor FX pairs.
4
According to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the US dollar was on one side of 89.2% of all global FX trades in April 2025. The euro and Japanese yen accounted for 28.9% and 16.8% of turnover respectively, while sterling’s share slipped to 10.2%.
1
The figures indicate each currency’s role in global trading but do not, by themselves, determine how individual pairs will perform.
Image 4: Major currency pairs
1. EUR/USD
The
EUR/USD
reflects the exchange rate between the euro (the official currency of the eurozone) and the US dollar (the world’s leading reserve currency). It was the world’s most traded currency pair in the BIS’s April 2025 survey, accounting for 21.2% of global OTC FX turnover. Traders sometimes refer to it informally as “Fiber.”
Its high trading activity generally supports deep liquidity and relatively tight bid-ask spreads, although actual spreads, commissions, financing charges, and execution quality vary between brokers and market conditions.
Relative monetary-policy expectations for the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank are key drivers of EUR/USD. For example, in 2022, the Fed began raising rates earlier and more rapidly than the ECB. Together with euro-area energy and growth concerns, this widening policy gap contributed to the euro’s depreciation, and the pair fell below parity for the first time since 2002.
2
Major economic data releases, such as US employment data and Eurozone inflation figures, can cause short-term volatility. Additionally, EUR/USD is often particularly active during the overlap between London and New York trading hours, although activity and spreads can fluctuate with market conditions.
2. GBP/USD
The
GBP/USD
pair, often referred to as “Cable,” represents the exchange rate between the pound sterling and the US dollar. It was the fourth-most-traded currency pair in the BIS’s April 2025 survey, accounting for 7.6% of global OTC FX turnover.
This pair can experience larger price movements than EUR/USD, although volatility varies over time.
Its principal influences include Bank of England (BoE) and Federal Reserve expectations, UK and US economic data, and broader market sentiment. UK employment figures, retail sales, and inflation reports can affect sterling, while comparable US releases can influence the dollar side of the pair. Events such as Brexit negotiations, UK fiscal announcements, and periods of political uncertainty have also previously produced notable price swings in GBP/USD.
3. USD/JPY
The
USD/JPY
currency pair represents the exchange rate between the US dollar and Japanese yen. It was the world’s second-most-traded currency pair in April 2025, accounting for 14.3% of global OTC FX turnover.
Relative Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan policy expectations — and the resulting difference between US and Japanese interest rates — are important influences on the pair. Japan’s historically very low and, until March 2024, negative policy rates helped establish the yen as a common funding currency for carry trades.
During 2022 to 2023, rapid Fed rate increases contrasted with the BoJ’s continued dovish stance, contributing to a wider yield differential and multi-decade highs in USD/JPY. Japan’s policy position has since changed: the BoJ ended negative rates in 2024 and raised its policy rate to around 1.0% in June 2026.
A positive interest-rate differential may generate financing income in some positions, but the amount depends on the product and provider. For retail CFDs, spread bets and rolling spot forex products in the UK, financing adjustments may differ substantially from central-bank policy rates.
Carry trades also involve significant risk. Exchange-rate movements can exceed any financing return, particularly when leverage is used. Carry-trade unwinding can also produce rapid yen appreciation. Although the yen has historically displayed safe-haven characteristics, it does not strengthen during every period of uncertainty; monetary policy, energy prices, capital flows, and possible official intervention can outweigh changes in risk sentiment.
4. USD/CHF
The USD/CHF tracks the exchange rate between the US dollar and the Swiss franc, sometimes referred to as the “Swissie.” It was among the most actively traded currency pairs in April 2025, accounting for approximately 4.9% of global
OTC
foreign-exchange turnover.
The Swiss franc is widely regarded as a safe-haven currency, supported by factors including Switzerland’s long-standing political and economic stability as well as historically low inflation. It may therefore attract demand during periods of heightened uncertainty, although this relationship isn’t consistent nor guaranteed.
USD/CHF is also influenced by monetary-policy expectations for the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and the US Federal Reserve. If markets expect US interest rates to remain higher than Swiss rates, this may support the dollar relative to the franc. However, economic data, risk sentiment, and possible SNB foreign-exchange intervention can outweigh the interest-rate differential and produce rapid price movements.
5. AUD/USD
Commonly referred to as the “Aussie,” the AUD/USD currency pair represents the exchange rate between the Australian dollar and the US dollar. It accounted for approximately 4.9% of global OTC FX turnover in April 2025.
Australia is a major exporter of commodities, including iron ore, gold, coal, and liquefied natural gas. Rising commodity prices — particularly iron ore and gold — and changes in Australia’s terms of trade can therefore influence the Australian dollar. Rising export prices may support the AUD, while falling prices may weigh on it, although this relationship isn’t automatic.
Relative monetary-policy expectations for the Reserve Bank of Australia and Federal Reserve are another important influence. A shift towards higher expected Australian interest rates relative to US rates may support AUD/USD, but economic growth, inflation, capital flows and wider market sentiment also affect the pair.
Due to Australia’s close trade links with China, AUD/USD is sometimes viewed as an indicator of Chinese demand and global risk appetite. It should not, however, be considered a reliable proxy for the entire Asia-Pacific economy.
6. USD/CAD
The USD/CAD currency pair represents the exchange rate between the US dollar and the Canadian dollar, often referred to as the “Loonie.” It’s heavily influenced by movements in commodity prices, as oil and other natural resources are among Canada’s most significant exports.
When oil and commodity prices rise, the Canadian dollar may strengthen, which then generally exerts downward pressure on USD/CAD. When prices fall, the CAD may weaken, causing the pair to rise. This relationship is not fixed: monetary policy, economic data, trade flows, and global risk sentiment can sometimes have a greater influence.
The pair is also sensitive to employment, inflation, and GDP data from Canada and the US, as well as relative policy expectations for the Bank of Canada (BoC) and the Federal Reserve. For example, if the BoC adopts a more hawkish tone while the Fed pauses rate hikes, this may support the Canadian dollar but does not guarantee that USD/CAD will fall.
In early 2016, oil prices slumped to decade lows and WTI crude traded below $30 per barrel amid high inventories, excess supply, and concerns about weakened demand. The oil decline contributed to pressure on the Canadian dollar, while USD/CAD briefly traded around 1.46 Canadian dollars per US dollar — the pair’s highest level since 2003. Oil was an important factor, but not the pair’s only driver.
3
7. NZD/USD
The NZD/USD currency pair measures the value of the New Zealand dollar (often known as the “Kiwi”) against the US dollar.
New Zealand’s export-driven economy relies heavily on dairy products as a share of national exports. As such, fluctuations in global dairy prices, overseas demand, and broader commodity-market conditions can affect the NZD’s performance, although their effects vary over time.
In addition to trade dynamics, monetary policy from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) and Federal Reserve plays a key role. New Zealand became the first country in the modern era to formally adopt inflation targeting in 1990. During periods when New Zealand has relatively higher interest rates, the NZD has sometimes been used as the higher-yielding currency in carry trade strategies. However, this has not always involved NZD/USD specifically, and New Zealand rates are not consistently higher than those of other economies.
Carry-trade demand can support NZD during stable market conditions, but such positions may be reversed rapidly when risk sentiment deteriorates. For UK CFDs, spread bets, and rolling spot forex products, any financing return also depends on the provider’s charges and adjustments rather than simply equalling the difference between central-bank policy rates.

8. EUR/GBP
The EUR/GBP currency pair reflects the value of the euro relative to the British pound.
For those looking to compare the relative economic strength of the eurozone versus the United Kingdom without direct exposure to the US dollar, EUR/GBP is a commonly followed cross-currency pair. Movements in this pair are often more subdued compared to others, making it suitable for traders who prefer lower volatility and more range-bound behaviour.
While the pair is influenced by interest rate expectations from the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of England (BoE), it also reacts strongly to evolving political developments. In particular, the post-Brexit trade and regulatory discussions between the UK and EU continue to influence sentiment and direction.
In essence, any movement on financial services alignment, customs cooperation, and trade frameworks can cause fluctuations in the pair — even in the absence of major economic data.
9. GBP/JPY
The GBP/JPY pair is one of the more volatile currency crosses in the forex market, combining the British pound’s sensitivity to news with the Japanese yen’s role as a global
safe haven
. Its volatility has made it a closely followed pair among traders interested in shorter-term price movements and wider trading ranges.
This currency pair is heavily influenced by changes in interest rate differentials between the BoE and the Bank of Japan (BoJ), as well as fluctuations in market sentiment. When investors are optimistic, the yen often weakens and GBP/JPY rises. During market uncertainty, capital may flow into the yen, sending the pair’s valuation lower.
10. EUR/AUD
The EUR/AUD currency pair pits the euro against the Australian dollar, offering traders a lens into the contrasting dynamics of a service-based European economy and a commodity-dependent Australia.
As previously mentioned, the Australian dollar is closely tied to the export performance of key raw materials — particularly iron ore, coal, and
gold
— which means global commodity price fluctuations often influence EUR/AUD.
Case in point: a surge in iron ore prices, driven by increased demand from China, can boost the Australian dollar, pushing EUR/AUD lower. Conversely, a drop in gold prices or weakening demand for natural resources may weigh on the AUD, causing the pair to rise.
11. GBP/CAD
The GBP/CAD currency pair tracks the exchange rate between the British pound and the Canadian dollar, offering insight into the economic interplay between a service-oriented UK and a resource-driven Canada. One of the major influences on the Canadian dollar is the price of crude oil, as Canada is one of the world’s largest oil exporters.
Hence, GBP/CAD is often reactive to changes in global energy demand, OPEC+ decisions, and oil price volatility. For instance, a sharp rise in crude oil prices — triggered by supply cuts or geopolitical tensions — can strengthen the Canadian dollar, causing GBP/CAD to fall.
Conversely, falling oil prices due to oversupply or slowing global demand can weaken CAD, pushing the pair higher.
12. EUR/CHF
The EUR/CHF currency pair reflects the close financial and geographical relationship between the eurozone and Switzerland.
While this pair tends to move within relatively narrow ranges due to strong economic ties, it can react sharply to shifts in eurozone confidence or unexpected market shocks. The Swiss franc’s reputation as a safe-haven currency means that during periods of political or financial stress, capital often flows into the franc, causing EUR/CHF to fall.
Traders often use this pair to gauge risk sentiment within Europe, particularly when seeking low-volatility setups or looking for early signals of market tension in the region. Central bank interventions, particularly from the Swiss National Bank (SNB), can also have an outsized impact due to Switzerland’s history of managing franc strength.

15. EUR/TRY
The EUR/TRY currency pair compares the euro with the Turkish lira, offering high volatility due to the contrast between the euro’s relative stability and the lira’s exposure to emerging-market risks.
The Turkish lira is highly sensitive to both internal and external factors such as inflation, political instability, and central bank credibility — often resulting in sharp and unpredictable price movements. As a result, EUR/TRY is often monitored by traders interested in high-volatility market conditions.
The euro side of the pair offers some degree of stability, given that it’s anchored by the economic weight and monetary policy of the European Central Bank (ECB). As a result, EUR/TRY is frequently used to trade on regional geopolitical developments, including tensions in the Middle East or shifts in EU-Turkey relations.
Traders should exercise caution: while large price movements can create opportunities, they can also magnify potential losses, particularly when leverage is used.
16. GBP/ZAR
GBP/ZAR — the rate between the British pound and the South African rand — is an exotic currency pair known for its high volatility and exposure to commodity market fluctuations.
Given that South Africa is a leading exporter of gold, platinum, and other minerals, the rand is particularly sensitive to global demand and pricing in the resource sector. As a result, shifts in commodity prices can drive significant movements in GBP/ZAR.

Currency Pair Correlation
Currency pairs rarely move in isolation. Because many pairs share a common currency or overlapping economic drivers, their price movements can be correlated — meaning they tend to move in the same direction (positive correlation) or in opposite directions (negative correlation) over a given period.
For example, EUR/USD and GBP/USD often show a positive correlation, since both pairs have the US dollar as the quote currency and can react similarly to broad dollar strength or weakness. USD/JPY, by contrast, can sometimes move inversely to EUR/USD during periods of broad-based dollar moves, though this relationship is not fixed and can shift with market conditions.
Correlation matters for risk management: holding two positively correlated pairs in the same direction effectively doubles exposure to the same underlying driver, while holding negatively correlated pairs can offset risk (or unintentionally cancel out a trading idea). Correlation between any two pairs is not static — it can strengthen, weaken, or reverse depending on which economic or policy driver is dominant at the time, so it’s worth checking periodically rather than assuming it holds indefinitely.
How to Choose Which Currency Pairs to Trade
Understanding currency pairs is foundational to navigating the forex market. The 16 pairs in this guide range from heavily traded US-dollar pairs to cross-currency pairs like EUR/GBP to emerging-market pairs such as EUR/TRY. Contrary to popular misconception, there’s no single pair that suits every trader. A more useful question is which pair’s behaviour matches your trading style, risk tolerance, and the time you have available to follow the market.
Scalping
Scalpers hold positions for seconds to minutes, aiming to capture small, frequent price movements. This style generally favours highly liquid major pairs — such as EUR/USD or USD/JPY — where tight spreads keep transaction costs low relative to the small moves being targeted. Scalping demands close, sustained attention to the screen and is generally considered a higher-intensity, higher-risk approach.
Swing Trading
Swing traders hold positions from several days to a few weeks, aiming to capture medium-term price swings tied to economic data, central-bank decisions, or shifting sentiment. Pairs with wider, clearer trading ranges — such as GBP/USD or AUD/USD — are often favoured for this style, since swing traders rely less on split-second execution and more on technical and fundamental analysis over a longer horizon.
Position Trading
Position traders hold trades for weeks to months, focusing on longer-term macro themes such as interest-rate cycles or structural shifts in trade flows. Pairs like USD/CAD or EUR/CHF, which are closely tied to identifiable macro drivers (oil prices, safe-haven flows), can suit this approach. Position trading generally requires more capital resilience to withstand short-term volatility while a longer-term thesis plays out.

Frequently Asked Questions
How Many Currency Pairs Are There in Forex?
There is no fixed number, since many currencies can be paired with one another. In practice, trading activity is concentrated in a smaller group. Market convention commonly discusses seven US-dollar majors, minor crosses, and emerging-market or exotic pairs, while the FCA uses only major and minor classifications for UK retail-CFD rules.
How Many Major Currency Pairs Are There?
Under common market convention, seven pairs are usually called majors: EUR/USD, USD/JPY, GBP/USD, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, USD/CAD, and NZD/USD. Under the FCA definition used for UK retail-CFD rules, however, a major pair is any pair formed from two of USD, EUR, JPY, GBP, CAD and CHF. This means AUD/USD and NZD/USD are FCA minor pairs, while crosses such as EUR/GBP and GBP/JPY are FCA major pairs.
4
What Is the Difference Between a Major and Minor Currency Pair?
Under common market terminology, major pairs generally refer to the seven leading US-dollar pairs, minor (cross) pairs generally combine widely traded currencies without the US dollar, and exotic pairs pair a widely traded currency with an emerging-market or smaller-economy currency. The FCA, however, defines a major pair as any pair formed from two of USD, EUR, JPY, GBP, CAD and CHF, and defines every other FX pair as minor — which is why market convention and FCA classification don’t always line up for the same pair.
4
What Are Currency Pair Nicknames, and Where Do They Come From?
Nicknames like Cable (GBP/USD), Fiber (EUR/USD), Loonie (USD/CAD), Kiwi (NZD/USD), Aussie (AUD/USD), and Swissie (USD/CHF) are informal market slang used by traders and financial media rather than official or regulatory terms. Many have historical origins — “Cable,” for instance, is linked to the transatlantic telegraph cable once used to relay GBP/USD rates between London and New York.

The right pair often depends on your trading style, risk tolerance, and market outlook. Swing traders often favour GBP/USD or AUD/USD for wider ranges and clearer technical patterns, while position traders may look to longer-term macro themes in pairs such as USD/CAD or EUR/CHF. See “How to Choose Which Currency Pairs to Trade” above for a fuller breakdown by trading style.
Which Currency Pairs Are Best for Beginners?
Beginners are often encouraged to prioritise currency pairs that combine stability, high liquidity, and low trading costs. EUR/USD is the most liquid pair with extensive data and news coverage; USD/JPY is known for consistent trends and relatively lower volatility; and GBP/USD offers more movement for those ready for slightly higher risk. These pairs tend to react predictably to economic releases, helping new traders learn without being overwhelmed by the erratic price swings often seen in exotic pairs.
Which Currency Pairs Are Most Volatile?
Emerging-market pairs such as EUR/TRY and GBP/ZAR can experience substantial volatility linked to inflation, policy uncertainty, political risk, and fluctuating liquidity. Among the conventionally recognised majors and crosses, GBP/JPY can also be volatile because it responds to both interest-rate differentials and changes in risk sentiment. Volatility varies over time and raises the risk of larger and faster price movements.
What Time of Day Are Currency Pairs Most Active?
Forex trades around the clock across overlapping sessions — broadly Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York. Activity and liquidity are generally highest during session overlaps, particularly the London–New York overlap (which affects EUR/USD and GBP/USD heavily) and the Tokyo–London overlap (relevant to USD/JPY and other yen pairs). Outside these overlaps, and during major public holidays in the relevant regions, liquidity and spreads can vary more than usual.
Why Are Currencies Always Traded in Pairs?
A currency’s value only has meaning relative to another currency — there’s no single, universal “price” for a currency on its own. Quoting currencies in pairs (e.g., EUR/USD) expresses how much of one currency is needed to buy a unit of the other, which is why forex trading is inherently a pairs-based market rather than one where individual currencies are bought or sold in isolation.
What Are Some Other Currency Pairs Worth Watching?
While this guide focuses on 16 pairs, some traders also monitor USD/CNH, EUR/JPY, AUD/JPY, USD/SEK, and USD/NOK. These pairs have different levels of liquidity, volatility, and trading cost. Their market labels may differ between sources, so UK retail clients should distinguish informal broker terminology from the FCA classification that applies to retail-CFD margin rules.
What Should You Look for When Choosing a Broker to Trade Currency Pairs?
Forex traders commonly consider factors such as spreads and other costs on the pairs they plan to trade, the provider’s product range, its regulatory status in the relevant jurisdiction, and the trading platforms available. UK retail clients should also check the provider’s margin requirements and whether a pair is treated as major or minor under applicable FCA rules. Execution quality and risk-management tools, such as stop-loss orders, may also be relevant. This is general information only and does not constitute a personal recommendation.

Beginner’s Guide to Indices Trading (Updated 2026)
Vantage Editorial Team >
5 August 2026
|
Academy

17 min read
Vantage Editorial Team >
View Profile
Vantage is a global, multi-asset broker with a team of in-house writers and market analysts who produce educational and insightful trading content for traders of all levels.
Indices are often mentioned in market news, but what exactly are they, and how can you trade them? Unlike individual stocks, an index tracks the performance of a wider group of assets, such as the S&P 500 or FTSE 100.
In this guide, you will learn how index trading works, what influences index movements, which major indices to know, and the potential advantages and risks of trading indices through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or contracts for difference (CFDs).
What Is Index Trading?
An index tracks the performance of a specified basket of securities or other assets, based on a predefined methodology. Indices may focus on a market, country, region, sector, company size, investment style, or asset class. For example, equity, bond, and commodity indices.
An index is a calculated benchmark and thus cannot normally be bought directly. Investors and traders can obtain exposure through products linked to it, such as index funds,
ETFs
, futures, options or CFDs. These instruments differ substantially in ownership, costs, leverage and risk.
What Affects The Price of Indices?
Indices are priced based on the securities they represent, according to their weighting methodology. For example, some indices weight companies by market capitalisation, while others are price weighted or equally weighted. Consequently, not every constituent has the same effect.
In a market-cap-weighted index, movements in the largest companies can have a substantial influence, while smaller constituents have less impact. Broad indices can reduce exposure to company-specific risk, but sector, country, and highly concentrated indices may offer much less diversification.
Index movements may be influenced by company earnings, economic growth expectations, interest rates, inflation, currencies, commodity prices, political developments, and changes in investor risk appetite.
Indeed, some popular indices such as the S&P 500 are widely used as benchmarks of their respective markets, although they are not complete measures of an economy.
As an index covers a basket of different assets, it is inherently more diversified than singular securities or equities, which renders it an effective way to increase portfolio
diversification
.
Some factors that can affect equity indices include:
Economic downturns
: During a recession or a period of weaker earnings expectations, equity indices may face downward pressure, causing their prices to fall. However, markets do not inevitably fall throughout a recession and may recover before economic data improve.
Interest rates
: Interest rate hikes can increase borrowing costs, which can in turn, lower the present value investors assign to future corporate earnings. Their effect varies according to economic conditions and market expectations.
Inflation
: High or unexpected
inflation
can raise business costs, reduce purchasing power, and prompt tighter monetary policy. Its effect typically differs across companies, sectors, and periods.
Geopolitical events
: Market indices can be impacted by geopolitical events, such as elections, conflicts, trade disputes, and diplomatic developments. These events can change an investor’s or trader’s expectations about economic policy, trade, energy supplies, and risk. If the market gets buoyed by positive developments, market indices can be potentially uplifted, too.
Top 5 Indices That are Popular Among Investors & Traders
If you’re looking to invest and/or trade indices, here are five popular indices to check out:
1. S&P 500
The Standard & Poor’s 500 Index (S&P 500) is perhaps one of the most well-known market indices. It measures the performance of 500 leading companies that are listed on major US stock exchanges, and is widely used as a benchmark for the US large-cap equity market. Take note that the index doesn’t simply contain the world’s 500 largest companies. Instead, companies must satisfy eligibility requirements relating to factors such as:
Market capitalisation
Liquidity
Public float
Financial viability
A decline of at least 20% from a recent market high is commonly described as a bear market. Conversely, a rise of at least 20% from a market low is often described as a bull market, although definitions and measurement periods can vary.
2. Nasdaq-100
Another popular market index is the Nasdaq-100, which tracks 100 of the largest domestic and international non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange, based on market capitalisation. It has a substantial technology weighting and most of this index’s constituents are tech companies, so the Nasdaq is often used as a technology-heavy market benchmark. However, it also includes companies from other industries and does not represent the entire technology sector.
3. FTSE 100
If you’re looking for UK indices instead, the FTSE 100 comprises 100 of highly capitalised, eligible UK companies listed on the London Stock Exchange (LSE). Also informally known as the ‘Footsie’, the FTSE 100 is widely used as a benchmark for the UK large-cap equity market”. However, as many of its constituents conduct extensive business overseas, its performance does not necessarily reflect conditions in the domestic UK economy alone.
4. Nikkei 225
For exposure to Asian equities, the Nikkei 225 is a popular choice as a benchmark for the Japanese equity market. It’s a price-weighted index consisting of 225 selected Japanese companies listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange’s Prime Market. Constituents are selected with reference to liquidity and sector balance, rather than company size alone.
5. Dow Jones Industrial Average
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, also known as the DJIA or “the Dow”, is among the oldest and widely followed stock indices in the world. Launched in 1986, it is a price-weighted measure of 30 prominent US blue-chip companies. The Dow is an influential benchmark of the US equity market, although its relatively small number of constituents makes it narrower than the S&P 500.
Trading Indices via CFDs
Since indices only track—but do not hold—any tradable securities, they cannot be directly purchased. Instead, investors and traders can obtain index exposure through instruments such as:
Exchange-traded funds (ETFs)
Contracts for difference (CFDs)
Index funds
Futures
Options
For index ETFs, this simply means purchasing shares of a fund that seeks to track an underlying index. One such example is the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY), which is designed to provide investment results that broadly correspond, before expenses, to the price and yield performance of the S&P 500. The return of your holdings may differ slightly from that of the index because of fees, tracking error, and market-price fluctuations.
Another way to trade indices is with index CFDs, which are derivative contracts that allow a trader to speculate on the price movements of an underlying market index, without owning the index or its constituent securities. CFDs are an advanced trading strategy that takes the form of an agreement between an investor and a trading brokerage. Both parties agree to exchange the difference in the value of an index between the time the contract opens and closes, subject to the provider’s terms.
Hence, if you expect the price of a referenced market to go up, you can open a long position. Alternatively, you can open a
short
position if you expect the price to fall.
As CFDs are leveraged products traded on margin, this means a trader deposits only part of the position’s total value. Leverage magnifies both potential gains and potential losses, while spreads, commissions, and financing charges can reduce returns.
Potential Benefits of Trading Index CFDs
Trading index CFDs can confer several potential benefits, such as:
Lower initial margin requirement:
CFDs can be traded on margin, which means investors can open a larger position with a smaller capital upfront. This allows CFDs to be traded even by those with relatively little starting capital. While this increases capital efficiency, it also increases risk.
Trade in any direction:
As explained above, trading index CFDs allow traders to go long and short without owning the underlying securities. That said, a greater range of possible positions does not necessarily increase the likelihood of making a profit.
Potential Risks of Trading Index CFDs
Index trading using CFDs is, of course, not without its downsides. These include:
Leveraged losses:
Relatively small market movements can produce substantial losses compared with the initial margin. A trader may lose all the margin committed and other funds held in the CFD account.
Margin close-out
: Arm yourself with discipline and sound knowledge. Failing to grasp margin management can quickly lead to significant losses. If account equity falls below the required level, positions may be closed automatically, potentially during unfavourable market conditions.
Complexity
: Achieving success in trading indices using CFDs requires an understanding of leverage, margin, financing costs, and rapid price movements.
Trading costs:
Spreads, commissions, and overnight financing charges (swap fees) can accumulate, particularly when positions are held for extended periods.
Tips For Index Trading
Indices trading can be a rewarding yet complex endeavor. Whether you are a beginner or looking to refine your approach, having a structured plan and a disciplined mindset is crucial. Below are some key tips to help you navigate market volatility, manage risk effectively, and make informed trading decisions.
Follow Relevant Market Developments
Index levels can be affected by economic data, company earnings, monetary policy and political or geopolitical events. Monitoring economic calendars and reliable news sources can help traders identify scheduled risks and understand potential sources of volatility.
However, news events cannot reliably predict market direction, and expected developments may already be reflected in prices.
Understand Different Forms of Analysis
Being able to interpret a price chart is important when trading indices. Besides price action, traders may also consider chart patterns,
indicators
, and other tools when planning entries, exits, and risk limits. Take note that these tools don’t guarantee accurate forecasts or profitable trades and should be combined with appropriate risk management.
Besides technical analysis, some traders also consider fundamental information and broader macroeconomic influences.
Select Appropriate Indices and Trading Instruments
As you’ve learnt by now, indices differ in their constituents, weighting methods, geographical exposure, sector concentration, and volatility. Before trading one, consider its composition, largest constituents, liquidity, trading hours, and currency exposure.
For instance, if you are highly keen on tech companies and already following important developments and new trends in that sector, you may be interested in trading a tech-focused index, like the Nasdaq-100, with a live trading account.
Explore Indices Trading Today
Trading and/or investing in indices can be one way to gain exposure to different types of asset classes and baskets of securities, without having to purchase individual stocks or commodities. Some investors also diversified their portfolio with indices. However, diversification would depend on the index’s composition and weighting, and does not prevent market losses.
Experienced traders who understand leverage and margin may also use CFDs to take long or short positions on an index. That said, CFDs are complex, high-risk instruments, and the ability to trade in either direction does not ensure returns under any market condition.
FAQs On Index Trading
Q1. What is indices trading?
A: Indices trading is the buying and selling of financial instruments whose value is linked to market indices. As an index is a calculated benchmark rather than an investable asset, traders obtain exposure through products such as ETFs, index funds, futures, options, or CFDs. Take note that these instruments differ substantially in ownership, leverage, costs, and risk.
Q2. What are some of the top market indices?
A: Some of the most widely known indices include the S&P 500, which tracks the top 500 US companies; the FTSE 100, which comprises 100 highly capitalised, eligible UK companies listed on the LSE; and the Nikkei 225, a price-weighted index that tracks 225 selected domestic stocks on the Tokyo Stock Exchange’s Prime Market. Constituents are chosen according to each index provider’s methodology and are not necessarily selected by size alone.
Q3. What are some of the factors that affect the prices of indices?
A: Strictly speaking, market indices do not have directly tradable prices. Instead, an equity index’s level changes in response to movements in its constituent stocks, according to the index’s weighting and calculation methodology. Relevant influences include company earnings, economic growth expectations, inflation, interest rates, currencies, commodity prices, and geopolitical events.
Q4. What are the potential pros and cons of trading indices through CFDs?
A: CFDs allow traders to take long or short positions while depositing only a portion of the position’s total exposure as margin. This can make capital use more flexible, but leverage magnifies losses as well as gains.
CFDs can also involve spreads, commissions, overnight financing charges, margin close-out and counterparty risk. Small adverse market movements can cause substantial losses relative to the initial margin. CFDs are complex, high-risk products and may be unsuitable for some retail traders.
Q5. What should traders consider before trading an index?
A. Traders should understand the index’s composition, weighting methodology, largest constituents, volatility, liquidity, and trading hours. They should also evaluate the chosen instrument’s costs, leverage, and margin requirements. Market news and technical analysis may provide useful context, but neither can reliably predict price movements. Position sizing and risk management remain essential.
RISK WARNING
: CFDs are complex financial instruments and carry a high risk of losing money rapidly due to leverage. You should ensure you fully understand the risks involved and carefully consider whether you can afford to take the high risk of losing your money before trading.

Forex CFDs: Overview, How it Works, and How to Trade
Vantage Editorial Team >
5 August 2026
|
Academy

Vantage Editorial Team >
View Profile
Vantage is a global, multi-asset broker with a team of in-house writers and market analysts who produce educational and insightful trading content for traders of all levels.
Forex CFDs are one of the most common trading tools you’ll find on your CFD trading platform. In this guide, we go through what forex CFDs are, how they work and how you can trade them.
Key Points
Forex CFDs (Contracts for Difference) are financial derivatives that enable investors to speculate on the price movements of currency pairs in the foreign exchange market without owning the actual currencies.
Forex CFDs work by mirroring the price fluctuations of currency pairs, which allows traders to make a return or a loss from the difference between the opening and closing prices, without the need to physically exchange currencies.
Forex CFDs are designed to provide traders and investors access to the foreign exchange market, the ability to go long or short, and the flexibility to trade on margin.
What Are Forex CFDs?
Forex contracts for difference (CFDs) are financial tools that allow you to speculate on the price movements of currency pairs. Forex CFDs work similarly to other CFDs, and they do not require you to own the physical currencies being traded.
Since the forex market is volatile, you can opt to trade forex CFDs as a trader and take advantage by speculating on both rising and falling prices. Unlike other instruments, forex CFDs give you the opportunity to take advantage of market opportunities, whether the markets are on an upward or downward trend, by speculating on the price movement.
However, as forex CFDs are leveraged instruments and traded on margin, traders need to understand that both profits and losses are magnified, manage their exposure carefully, and maintain sufficient margin to avoid forced position closures.
Before you venture into forex CFDs, you need to understand how the underlying forex market works. Let’s look at some vital elements of forex CFDs below:
5 Must-Know Elements of Forex CFDs
Forex CFD trading involves more than simply predicting whether a currency will rise or fall. Understanding these core elements can help you navigate the market with greater confidence.
1. Currency Pairs
Foreign exchange trades happen in currency pairs. That way, you’re buying one currency of the pair while simultaneously selling the other.
Take the
GBP/USD
pair as an example. You have the base currency on the left, which is the GBP. This base currency is also what you’re buying. You have the quote currency USD on the right, which is what you’re selling.
So, if the GBP/USD pair trades at 1.4400, that means it takes USD1.44 to buy 1.0 GBP. If the price of this pair moves up to 1.4800, that now means you’ll have to pay more US dollars (at USD1.48) to buy 1.0 GBP.
2. Lots
To standardise the forex market, currency pairs trade in lots. In essence, lots are batches of currency. Since price changes in currency markets are often small, lots typically have to be significant in order to take full advantage of these movements.
In forex, a standard lot is 100,000 units. But of course, you can choose to trade in fractional lots. Most brokers offer mini (10,000 units), micro (1000 units), and
nano
(100 units) lots.
3. Margin
In CFD forex trading, margin refers to the amount of money that a trader needs to have in their account to open and maintain a leveraged position. It is only a fraction of the position’s total value and does not limit the trader’s potential losses.
Forex CFD traders should note that if their account equity falls below the required margin level, it would trigger a margin call and they would typically be alerted to add funds or reduce their exposure.
4. Pip
A pip, short for “percentage in point”, is a unit of measurement used to express changes in the value of a currency pair.
It’s usually defined as the smallest amount by which the value of a currency pair can change, and it’s usually the fourth decimal place of the exchange rate. For example, if the exchange rate for
EUR/USD
changes from 1.2500 to 1.2505, this is equivalent to a movement of 5 pips.
Learning about pips and how to calculate them can potentially help with position sizing. Vantage Markets offers a free forex calculator to measure your potential profits, losses, and more
here
.
5. Bid-Ask Spread
The bid-ask spread is the difference between the highest price a buyer is willing to pay (aka the bid price) and the lowest price a seller is willing to accept (i.e., the ask price) for a particular currency pair. It’s the cost of trading and generally represents the profit that a broker earns on a transaction.
A narrower spread can indicate a more liquid market and lower transaction costs, while a wider spread is typically representative of a less liquid market and higher transaction costs.
What’s the Difference Between CFD and Forex?
Forex trading is different from CFD trading. For those wondering about the difference between trading forex and CFDs, it’s important to understand each market’s unique characteristics and trading mechanisms.
Here are some fundamental differences between these two instruments:
Forex trading is limited to currencies, while CFD trading covers more types of assets. For example, you can trade commodities, indices, futures, stocks, and even cryptocurrencies using CFDs.
Regardless of the currency pairs, you choose to trade, lot sizes are uniform in all forex markets. For CFDs, however, you can trade different contract sizes across various asset classes.
Although spreads are a common trading cost in forex and CFD trading, other charges may also apply. Depending on the broker, account type, and instrument, traders may pay commissions and financing charges for positions held overnight. Other costs, such as currency-conversion or account fees, may also apply.
If you’re interested in learning more about it, check out Vantage Markets’ guide on the differences between
CFD and Forex
trading.
4 Types of Forex Instruments, Including Forex CFDs
There are several types of forex instruments popular among traders:
1. Rolling Spot Forex CFDs
Rolling spot forex CFDs are cash-settled derivatives that track movements in a currency pair’s exchange rate. They generally have no fixed expiration and are automatically rolled over until the trader closes the position, although overnight financing charges (swap fees) may apply. Spot forex CFD trading is typically limited to the broker’s available market hours
2. FX Options
An FX option grants traders the right, without the obligation, to buy or sell a currency pair at a predetermined exchange rate on or before a specified expiry date, depending on the option’s terms. The options buyer generally pays a premium for this right
3. FX Forwards
An FX forward is an agreement that enables traders to exchange a specific amount of a currency pair at a predetermined price on a set future date.
4. FX Swaps
An FX swap involves exchanging a specified amount of one currency for another at a predetermined rate on a specific future date. This exchange is agreed to be reversed at a predetermined rate on a later date.
How CFD Forex Trading Works
Forex CFDs work similarly to CFDs in other asset classes. It also comes with all the features, benefits, and risks of different CFD types. For example, you can still take advantage of market opportunities in a bull or bear market using CFDs, as long as your price predictions are accurate.
Let’s look at some features present in forex CFD markets.
1. Leverage in Forex CFDs
Forex CFDs are leveraged instruments, which means you can increase your exposure in the forex exchange market without having to pay the full price of the asset from the start.
Say, for instance, that you’d like to trade the USD/GBP forex pair.
You may have to purchase an entire lot, which is 100,000 units. Some traders don’t have enough capital to buy a lot. However, with a forex CFD, a trader can put up just 5% of the cost (or less, when trading major FX pairs) to control a position for the size of one lot.
Using leverage in forex CFDs presents both massive opportunities and risks. Your profit and loss are still calculated on the full size of your position. In other words, while you can make huge profits trading CFDs, you can also make huge losses that exceed your capital.
2. Margin in Forex CFDs
Margin is the amount of money a broker requires as collateral to open and maintain a leveraged forex CFD position. Two commonly used margin terms are:
Initial margin (or deposit margin)
Maintenance margin
Initial margin is pretty straightforward. It’s the amount required to open a leveraged CFD position in the forex markets.
Maintenance margin is the minimum level of account equity to keep your forex CFD positions open. If your trading losses cause your account equity to fall below the required level, you may receive a margin call or notification asking you to deposit extra funds or reduce your exposure.
If the account equity reaches the margin close-out level, which is 50% for retail clients, the broker may automatically close one or more positions. A broker is not necessarily required to issue a margin call before doing so
3. Hedging in Forex CFDs
More experienced traders may use forex CFDs to hedge their existing currency positions. Hedging involves holding two (or more) open positions on one asset, with the intention to simultaneously to offset some or all of the risk associated with one position using any potential profits from the other(s).
However, a hedge may not eliminate the risk completely, and it can also reduce potential profits and create additional trading and financing costs. Brokers may also treat opposing positions differently, so traders should check whether their platform permits separate hedged positions or automatically nets them.
4. Fees in Forex CFD
Forex CFD trading can involve several costs and fees. Let’s take a quick look at them:
Spreads:
The spread is the difference between the bid and ask prices of a forex pair. Every forex CFD trade you make pays a spread. You can consider opting for currency pairs with narrower spreads because any slight movement in favour of your predictions means you can take advantage of market opportunities.
Commissions:
Depending on your broker, account type, and jurisdiction, you may also pay a commission when you open or close a forex CFD position. Take note that some brokerage accounts combine commissions with narrower spreads.
Overnight financing:
Positions kept open beyond the broker’s daily cut-off time may incur an overnight financing or rollover adjustment. The account may be debited—or, in some circumstances, credited—depending on factors such as the currencies involved, the direction of the position, applicable interest rates and the broker’s charges. This adjustment does not depend on whether the trade is profitable.
Other charges:
Depending on the broker and services used, additional costs may include currency-conversion fees, inactivity fees, guaranteed stop premiums, or platform and market-data subscription fees.
How to Trade Forex CFDs
If you want to start trading forex CFDs today, here are some quick steps to get started.
Open and fund your trading account
Develop a trading strategy or trading style
Choose your currency pair
Open your first forex CFD position
Monitor and close it
1. Create and Fund Your Trading Account
Setting up a trading account for your Forex CFDs can be done in a few steps. Choose a broker and follow the steps to open an account on their website. Once you’ve added verification details like your ID and proof of address for account approval, you’ll then be able to access and explore the forex market via CFDs.
To begin trading, choose your preferred deposit method (card/bank transfer) to fund your trading account.
2. Develop a Trading Strategy
A trading strategy is how you manage your risk and plan how to use your capital to make trades. It can also help you determine acceptable losses and profits. Leverage fundamental and technical analysis to decide on your chosen forex pair before opening or closing a CFD position.
3. Choose Your Currency Pair
Choose currency pairs that suit your strategy, risk tolerance, and trading hours. Depending on your broker and place of residence, you may be able to trade them through rolling spot forex or CFDs that track spot exchange rates, as well as through forex options. You can start with a single pair or hold positions in several currency pairs simultaneously, although trading correlated pairs may increase your overall exposure.
Some popular currency pairs you can pick from include:
EUR/USD (euro/US dollar)
USD/CNY (US dollar/Chinese Yuan)
USD/CHF (US dollar/Swiss franc)
AUD/USD (Australian dollar/US dollar)
4. Open Your First Forex CFD Position
On the trading platform, select your chosen currency pair, position size, and trade direction. Buy the pair (aka going long) if you expect the base currency to rise in value against the quote currency. Or sell (short) the base currency if you expect the value of the quote currency to rise.
Consider placing a stop-loss order to limit potential losses and a take-profit order to close the position if it reaches your profit target. These orders can help manage risk, but standard stop-loss orders may be executed at a less favorable price during volatile or illiquid market conditions.
5. Monitor Your First Position and Close It
Monitor your open position, available margin, unrealized profit or loss, and any associated costs through your trading platform. Depending on the platform, you may also be able to receive price or trade alerts through push notifications, email, or SMS.
To close the position manually, select the open trade and submit a closing order. Your final profit or loss will depend on the price movement, position size, spread, financing charges and any other applicable fees.
As CFDs use leverage, losses can accumulate rapidly and your provider may close positions automatically if your account equity falls below its margin requirements.
Explore Forex CFDs Today
Forex CFDs allow traders to speculate on movements in currency-pair prices without owning the underlying currencies. Always remember that CFDs are leveraged products, so both profits and losses are based on the full value of the position, and losses can occur rapidly.
If CFD trading is appropriate for your circumstances, you can practice trading with virtual credit using the
demo account
. Additionally, you can trade CFDs for other asset classes such as commodities,
shares
, and
ETFs
with Vantage Markets.

How to Paper Trade on TradingView: A Step-by-Step Guide (2027)
Vantage Editorial Team >
